claims.text: A thin, coherent Ni-based γ/γ′ layer can serve as a transition medium between HEA layers.
The Ni-based γ/γ′ transition layer will mediate a shift from diffusion-dominated creep to dislocation-dominated creep.
The coherent interface will block diffusive atomic rearrangements.
The coherent interface will favor dislocation interactions.
Conventional HEA multilayers predominantly have incoherent or diffusively modified interfaces with poorly controlled coherency.
Depositing a thin Ni-based γ/γ′ alloy layer between HEA layers can produce the proposed transition medium.
Lower applied stresses favor diffusion-mediated creep.
Higher applied stresses drive dislocation activity.
The coherency of the Ni-based γ/γ′ layer provides a well-defined interface that alters local diffusion rates.
The coherency of the Ni-based γ/γ′ layer alters dislocation motion.
The coherent γ′ phase restricts atomic diffusion and reduces diffusion-mediated creep.
The coherent γ′ phase acts as a barrier to dislocation movement.
Applied stress will determine the dominant creep mechanism in the presence of the transition layer.
At lower stresses, the transition layer will reduce diffusion-mediated creep rate relative to HEA multilayers without the layer.
At higher stresses, the transition layer will increase dislocation-mediated deformation relative to HEA multilayers without the layer.
HEA multilayers without the coherent transition layer typically exhibit a gradual or unclear transition between diffusion and dislocation creep.
The effect depends on the thickness and coherency of the Ni-based layer.
Chemical incompatibility or significant lattice mismatch may prevent the effect from transferring to all HEA systems.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says the coherent γ′ phase impedes dislocation movement, whereas the predicted outcome asserts increased dislocation-mediated deformation at high stress. The hypothesis does not explain how a dislocation barrier produces an increase in deformation rather than merely making dislocation creep relatively dominant after diffusion is suppressed.
